title: Reusable Workflows & Composite Actions
subtitle: DRY your CI — define a workflow once and call it from any repository or multiple workflows

content.text: When you have 5 repositories that all deploy Node.js APIs, you end up with the same 80-line workflow file copy-pasted 5 times. When you need to update the Node.js version or add a new security step, you have to update all 5 files. Reusable workflows solve this: define the workflow once in a shared repository, call it from every other repo. Update in one place, applied everywhere.

content.code:
name: Shared Deploy Workflow

# workflow_call makes this workflow callable by other workflows
on:
  workflow_call:
    # Inputs the caller provides
    inputs:
      environment:
        required: true
        type: string
        description: 'Deployment target (staging | production)'
      image_tag:
        required: true
        type: string
      node_version:
        required: false
        type: string
        default: '20'

    # Secrets the caller must pass through
    # They are never exposed — just forwarded
    secrets:
      DEPLOY_TOKEN:
        required: true
      DATABASE_URL:
        required: false

    # Outputs the caller can use
    outputs:
      deployment_url:
        description: 'The deployed application URL'
        value: ${{ jobs.deploy.outputs.url }}

jobs:
  deploy:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    environment: ${{ inputs.environment }}
    outputs:
      url: ${{ steps.deploy.outputs.url }}

    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4

      - uses: actions/setup-node@v4
        with:
          node-version: ${{ inputs.node_version }}
          cache: 'npm'

      - run: npm ci
      - run: npm test

      - name: Deploy
        id: deploy
        env:
          DEPLOY_TOKEN: ${{ secrets.DEPLOY_TOKEN }}
          ENVIRONMENT: ${{ inputs.environment }}
          IMAGE_TAG: ${{ inputs.image_tag }}
        run: |
          URL=$(./scripts/deploy.sh $ENVIRONMENT $IMAGE_TAG)
          echo "url=$URL" >> $GITHUB_OUTPUT

name: Deploy
он:
  push:
    branches: [main]

jobs:
  deploy-staging:
    uses: myorg/shared-workflows/.github/workflows/shared-deploy.yml@main
    # ↑ org/repo/path@ref — can be a branch, tag, or SHA
    with:
      environment: staging
      image_tag: ${{ github.sha }}
      node_version: '22'
    secrets:
      DEPLOY_TOKEN: ${{ secrets.STAGING_DEPLOY_TOKEN }}

  deploy-production:
    needs: deploy-staging
    uses: myorg/shared-workflows/.github/workflows/shared-deploy.yml@main
    with:
      environment: production
      image_tag: ${{ github.sha }}
    secrets:
      DEPLOY_TOKEN: ${{ secrets.PROD_DEPLOY_TOKEN }}
      DATABASE_URL: ${{ secrets.PROD_DATABASE_URL }}

  notify:
    needs: deploy-production
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - run: |
          echo "Deployed to: ${{ needs.deploy-production.outputs.deployment_url }}"

# A composite action bundles multiple steps into one reusable action
# Useful for the 'checkout + setup-node + npm ci' boilerplate

name: Setup Project
description: Checkout, setup Node.js, and install dependencies

inputs:
  node-version:
    description: 'Node.js version'
    default: '20'

runs:
  using: composite
  steps:
    - uses: actions/checkout@v4

    - uses: actions/setup-node@v4
      with:
        node-version: ${{ inputs.node-version }}
        cache: 'npm'

    - name: Install dependencies
      shell: bash
      run: npm ci

---
# Using the composite action in any workflow:
jobs:
  build:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: ./.github/actions/setup-project
        with:
          node-version: '22'
      # Now directly run build/test — setup is handled
      - run: npm run build

content.text: Reusable workflows run as separate jobs; composite actions run as steps within a job. Use reusable workflows when you want an independent, isolated execution with its own environment and permissions. Use composite actions when you want to group steps within a job — they share the runner environment, can access files created by previous steps, and don't add job overhead.

questions.question: You have 10 repos that all use the same CI workflow. You update the reusable workflow to add a security scan step. What happens to those 10 repos?
options: Nothing — they keep using the old version until manually updated
They get the update on their next workflow run, because they reference @main which always points to the latest commit
GitHub sends a PR to each repo with the updated workflow
The calling workflows break and must be re-saved to pick up changes
questions.explanation: When you reference a reusable workflow with @main (a branch), callers always use the latest commit on that branch. Update the shared workflow, push to main, and the next time any caller workflow runs, it uses the new version automatically — including your new security step. This is the power of centralized reusable workflows. If you want stability instead, callers can pin to a specific tag like @v2.0.0 and only update deliberately.

faq.q: Can a reusable workflow call another reusable workflow?
faq.a: Yes — reusable workflows can be nested up to 4 levels deep. You can have a 'deploy' workflow that calls a 'build' workflow and a 'notify' workflow. However, each level adds job overhead. For simple step reuse, composite actions are lighter. Use nested workflow_call for genuinely independent, multi-job phases.

examples: Large tech companies maintain a 'platform' repository with organization-wide reusable workflows for security scanning, testing, and deployment. Every team's repo calls these — compliance and best practices are enforced automatically without each team needing to understand them

The @main reference is both a feature and a risk: updating the shared workflow instantly affects all 10 repos. Organizations often maintain @v1, @v2 tags and give teams control over when to migrate, just like a public npm package
